guideTitle: 6 Best Electric Knife Sharpeners Under $100 in 2026
metaDescription: Six electric knife sharpeners compared at a higher budget cap, from belt-driven systems to guided diamond slots, with no prices in the copy.
introParagraphs: Raising the cap to this level lets two very different designs into the same list. Most picks are guided slot sharpeners with diamond wheels, but the Work Sharp MK2 uses flexible abrasive belts and a two-speed motor, which puts it in a separate category from the Narcissus S809 3-Stage Sharpener or the Hrevzon 3-Stage Sharpener. Knowing which family you want is the first decision.  Reading the whole list first will save you from buying a belt system when you only need a slot, or the other way round.

We evaluated each pick on its abrasive, angle control, scope of blades, and how clearly the listing states what is excluded. The Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener publishes 360, 600 and 1000 grit stages, the KAZRBEP 5-in-1 Sharpener offers three speeds and an angle stop to 32.5 degrees, and the Work Sharp E2 Kitchen Sharpener lists serrated knives. All rankings rest on product specs and buyer feedback, not lab measurement.

Prices stay out of the copy, because they change. What spending toward this cap tends to buy is either a recognized sharpening brand, a longer warranty, or a belt system that reaches pocket knives and garden tools as well as the kitchen block.

products.name: Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener
products.description:
The Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener sits apart from every slot sharpener here. Instead of fixed wheels, it uses flexible belts that conform to the edge of the blade, and the listing says they can sharpen outdoor tools, lawn mower blades, pocket and kitchen knives, serrated knives and scissors. It is billed as an improvement on the original MK, built for sharpening every edge you own.

A two-speed motor gives light control for fine work and more power for axes and garden tools. An edge guide supports the knife all the way to the tip, which helps keep the angle repeatable. The company states a 3-year warranty and says it designs and calibrates the machines in Ashland, Oregon.

The flexibility has a cost in learning. Where the Narcissus S809 3-Stage Sharpener asks only that you pull a knife through a slot, the MK2 expects some technique and attention to how the belt meets the edge. Compared with the Work Sharp E2 Kitchen Sharpener, it reaches far beyond the kitchen drawer. If you own pocket knives and shears as well as kitchen knives, this is the strongest choice here.
products.bestFor: Hobbyists who sharpen pocket knives, scissors and garden tools as well as kitchen knives.
pros: Belts conform to many kinds of edges
Two speeds for light or heavy work
Edge guide supports the knife to the tip
Three-year warranty is stated
cons: Needs more technique than a slot sharpener
More machine than a kitchen-only user needs

products.name: Work Sharp E2 Kitchen Sharpener
products.description:
The Work Sharp E2 Kitchen Sharpener is the kitchen-only sibling of the belt-driven MK2. You pull a dull blade through guided slots, and the listing says the electric motor and design do the rest, so no angle needs to be held and no skill is needed. It names chef, santoku, paring, utility and serrated knives among the blades it restores.

The small countertop footprint tucks into a drawer or cabinet. The listing does not give grit numbers, a stage count or an angle figure, so the case for it rests on the brand and the simple concept. Serrated support should be handled with care, as many makers restrict teeth to a fine stage.

Compared with the Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener, it tells you less about its wheels but is simpler to start with. Compared with the Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener, it trades range for ease. It suits busy kitchens where a quick pull before dinner is the whole goal.
products.bestFor: Busy home cooks who want a guided sharpener from a sharpening brand.
pros: Guided slots need no angle skill
Listing names chef, paring and serrated knives
Compact enough for a kitchen drawer
Made by a recognized sharpening brand
cons: No stage count or grit detail in the listing
Limited ways to tune the result

products.name: Narcissus S809 3-Stage Sharpener
products.description:
The Narcissus S809 3-Stage Sharpener splits the work into coarse slots for repair, fine slots for honing and polish slots for a burr-free finish. Diamond wheels cut the steel, and fixed-angle pieces in each slot keep the knife at 20 degrees. The listing quotes about 40 seconds for a like-new edge.

The maker argues for 20 degrees as the best angle for daily household work, since it stands up to hard vegetables and the occasional bump on bone or a board. An open-design port is provided for scissors, axes and similar tools, and the listing mentions straight, serrated, stainless and ceramic knives. As always, confirm serrated and scissors handling in the manual.

Unlike the KAZRBEP 5-in-1 Sharpener, it has no speed control, and unlike the Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener it has a single angle. It is the straightforward answer for a Western knife block that wants a finish stage.
products.bestFor: Western knife owners who want a polish stage and no settings to learn.
pros: Three stages from repair to polish
Fixed 20 degree pieces remove guesswork
Diamond wheels for stainless and ceramic
Open port for scissors and axes
cons: Serrated and scissor claims need checking

products.name: Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener
products.description:
The Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener is unusually specific about its three stages. Stage one is 360 grit diamond for long-neglected edges, stage two is 600 grit diamond for routine sharpening, and stage three is 1000 grit resin to polish and remove burrs. The listing recommends starting at stage two for weekly upkeep.

A 20 degree guide holds the blade from heel to tip, so beginners avoid uneven edges. You place the heel in the slot and pull to the tip, making two to five passes per side, and a typical touch-up takes 40 to 60 seconds. A removable magnetic collector contains the filings and a non-slip base steadies the machine.

The listing limits it to straight-edge chef, santoku and paring knives and says not to use it on scissors, which is refreshingly direct. Compared with the Hrevzon 3-Stage Sharpener, it provides more numbers. Compared with the Narcissus S809 3-Stage Sharpener, it offers a resin polish. It is the one to choose if you like to know your grit.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a clear, numbered grit routine for straight knives.
pros: Grits of 360, 600 and 1000 are stated
Heel-to-tip 20 degree guide
Magnetic collector contains filings
Listing clearly excludes scissors

products.name: Hrevzon 3-Stage Sharpener

specList.label: Technique
specList.value: Glide 10 to 15 seconds, repeat 3 to 4 times

products.description:
The Hrevzon 3-Stage Sharpener delivers a coarse stage to revive dull blades, a fine stage to maintain the edge and a polish stage for a smooth finish. All three use diamond, and the angle is set at 20 degrees. The listing says to glide the knife backward through each slot for 10 to 15 seconds and repeat three to four times.

Four non-slip silicone pads keep it from sliding or buzzing across the counter, which the listing ties to safe, quiet operation. It handles straight-edge chef, paring and boning knives. Serrated knives and scissors are not mentioned.

Compared with the Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener, it keeps the same format but skips the grit numbers. Compared with the KAZRBEP 5-in-1 Sharpener, it keeps things simpler. It is a plain, quiet diamond sharpener for everyday knives.
products.bestFor: People who want a quiet, steady diamond sharpener for chef knives.
pros: Three stages with diamond abrasives
Four silicone pads cut vibration
Clear glide time and repeat guidance
Handles chef, paring and boning knives

products.name: KAZRBEP 5-in-1 Sharpener
products.description:
The KAZRBEP 5-in-1 Sharpener is the most adjustable slot unit in the list. It has three speeds on an LCD, a three-stage diamond system and a removable ceramic polishing bar for shaped tools. A spring-loaded guide follows the blade to hold the angle, with a 20 degree clamp and a stop that extends to 32.5 degrees.

The listing says to clip the knife in the slot, slide once, and repeat three to five times per slot. A bottom swarf plate collects chips and removable parts ease cleanup. It claims straight, serrated, cleaver and ceramic knives, plus scissors and axes, so verify each use in the manual.

It asks more of you than the Hrevzon 3-Stage Sharpener. Against the Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener it is simpler but narrower. It suits buyers who like dialing in a result and own a few thick blades.
products.bestFor: Buyers who like dialing in speed and angle on a slot sharpener.
pros: Three speeds on an LCD display
Spring-loaded guide holds the angle
Angle stop extends to 32.5 degrees
Swarf plate eases cleanup
cons: More settings than a first-timer needs

buyingCriteria.explanation: Slot sharpeners pull a blade through fixed wheels, which is quick and repeatable. A belt system like the Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener lets flexible belts conform to the edge, so it reaches axes, shears and pocket knives. The belt approach needs technique and costs more learning time. Choose slots for kitchen knives and belts when your toolbox is broader.  Keep in mind that a belt wears and needs replacing over time, while slot wheels last through many knives.

Grit numbers tell you how much metal each stage removes. The Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener lists 360 and 600 grit diamond and 1000 grit resin, while the Hrevzon 3-Stage Sharpener lists diamond without numbers. Diamond cuts hard steel faster than softer abrasives. Use the coarsest stage only when the edge is damaged.  Skipping straight to the finest stage on a lightly dull knife is both faster and kinder to the steel.

A guide keeps every pass consistent. The Bryxelia and Narcissus S809 hold 20 degrees, the KAZRBEP offers a stop to 32.5 degrees, and the MK2 uses an edge guide that supports the knife to the tip. If you own Japanese knives made for a finer edge, think twice about a fixed-20 unit. For Western knives, 20 degrees is a durable default.  Whatever the number, consistency from heel to tip matters more than the exact degree, since an uneven angle leaves a wavy edge.

Read the exclusions before the claims. The Bryxelia excludes scissors, the Work Sharp E2 Kitchen Sharpener lists serrated knives, and the KAZRBEP claims axes and ceramic. Makers often restrict serrations to a fine stage. If a listing is silent on scissors, assume they are not supported.  A model that says plainly what it will not sharpen is usually the more trustworthy listing.

A longer warranty is a sign the maker expects the motor to last. The Work Sharp MK2 states 3 years, and the brand designs and calibrates in Ashland, Oregon. Others only mention customer support. For a tool you plan to keep, support matters.  Brand support also affects how easy it is to find replacement parts or get a unit looked at if the motor fails.

Pads, bases and collectors protect the edge and the counter. The Hrevzon lists four silicone pads, the Bryxelia a magnetic collector, and the KAZRBEP a swarf plate. Wipe filings after each session. A rocking base ruins an angle.  Wipe the work surface too, since fine filings can get onto cutting boards and fabric.

howWeEvaluated.title: Sharpening system
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated belt and slot designs. The Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener uses belts and a two-speed motor, while the rest use fixed wheels. Slot units were judged on stage count and abrasive, with the Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener leading on stated grits.  The Narcissus S809 3-Stage Sharpener and Hrevzon 3-Stage Sharpener were treated as the plain diamond baseline.

howWeEvaluated.title: Angle repeatability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at how each model holds the blade: 20 degree pieces, a spring-loaded guide on the KAZRBEP 5-in-1 Sharpener, and an edge guide on the MK2. Repeatability matters more than the number.  The MK2's edge guide counted as angle control even though it works differently from fixed pieces.

howWeEvaluated.title: Scope and honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared what each listing covers and what it excludes. The Bryxelia is explicit about scissors, the Work Sharp E2 Kitchen Sharpener lists serrated knives, and the MK2 reaches the most tools. Broad claims were marked for a manual check.  Claims such as axes and garden tools were credited only where the listing named them.

howWeEvaluated.title: Support and warranty
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted stated warranties and brand background. The MK2 lists 3 years. Others offer customer support with no length stated.  Where no warranty length was given, we left it unscored rather than assuming.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability and cleanup
howWeEvaluated.description: Silicone pads, collectors and swarf plates were compared. These are based on product specs and buyer feedback, not lab tests. The Hrevzon leads on pads and the Bryxelia on its collector.  Positioning wise, the MK2 leads on range, the Bryxelia on detail, and the Hrevzon on quiet stability.

howToChoose.intro: Two ways to put an edge on steel.

cards.label: Belts
cards.text: Flexible belts conform to the edge. The Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener adds a two-speed motor and an edge guide. It reaches more tools but asks for technique.

howToChoose.note: Slots for a kitchen routine, belts for a workshop.

faq.q: How do I choose between these sharpeners?
faq.a: Decide whether you want slots or belts. For kitchen knives, a slot unit like the Narcissus S809 3-Stage Sharpener or Bryxelia 3-Stage Sharpener is quick and repeatable. For pocket knives, shears and garden tools, the Work Sharp MK2 Belt Sharpener has more reach. For a guided kitchen option from a sharpening brand, choose the Work Sharp E2 Kitchen Sharpener.  Ask yourself which tools you actually sharpen each year before you pay for range.

faq.q: Are belt sharpeners harder to use?
faq.a: They ask for more technique because you present the edge to a moving belt. The Work Sharp MK2 has an edge guide that supports the knife to the tip, which helps. Slot sharpeners remove most of the skill. If you want minimal learning, stay with slots.  A few practice passes on an old knife build confidence quickly.

The Work Sharp MK2 and E2 list serrated knives, and the KAZRBEP claims them. The Bryxelia and Hrevzon do not mention them. Makers often limit serrations to a fine stage. Never use a coarse stage on teeth.  If bread knives matter most, a belt unit or a manual tapered rod is usually the safer route.

faq.q: Is 20 degrees right for my knives?
faq.a: It suits most Western knives and is durable. Thin Japanese knives often sit near 15 degrees or below and may need an adjustable unit. The KAZRBEP offers a stop to 32.5 degrees for heavier blades. Check the manufacturer's angle if you know it.  A thinner edge slices better but chips more easily, so match the angle to how you cut.

Only when the knife struggles on soft skins or herbs. The Bryxelia listing suggests starting at stage two for weekly upkeep. Use the coarsest stage rarely. Over-sharpening shortens a blade's life.  A light touch-up now saves a heavy repair later.

Empty the collector or swarf plate after each session and wipe the unit dry. The Bryxelia and KAZRBEP both list one. The Work Sharp MK2 uses belts that wear and can be replaced per the maker. Store in a dry drawer.  Keep spare belts on hand if you buy a belt system.

faq.q: Is a warranty worth caring about?
faq.a: Yes for a tool you plan to keep. The MK2 states 3 years. Others mention support without a length. A warranty signals the maker expects the motor to last.
